title: Cerebellar form of multiple system atrophy: A case report
case_prompt: A 51-year-old man presented with a two-year history of progressive limb ataxia, gait disturbance, urinary problems, and orthostatic dizziness. He had no past medical or family history of neurologic disease and denied tobacco, alcohol, or long-term medication use. He reported no visual symptoms, dysphagia, erectile dysfunction, sleep disorders, memory loss, or cognitive decline. On examination, he was alert and oriented with normal vital signs. Neurologic findings included cerebellar dysarthria, gait ataxia, a positive Romberg sign with multidirectional oscillations, normal deep-tendon reflexes, full muscle strength, intact sensation, negative Babinski and Hoffman signs, and dysmetria with dyschronometria on coordination testing. There was no rigidity, bradykinesia, tremor, nystagmus, or ophthalmoplegia. Tilt-table testing revealed orthostatic hypotension after three minutes of standing. Brain MRI showed on axial T2-weighted sequences a cruciform pattern of high intensity within the pons and on sagittal T1 and FLAIR sequences marked cerebellar atrophy with enlargement of the fourth ventricle. PET-CT demonstrated reduced metabolism in the cerebellar hemispheres compared with the cerebral hemispheres. Routine laboratory tests, including blood count, thyroid hormones, electrolytes, renal and hepatic function, blood alcohol level, and vitamins B and E, were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Probable MSA-C supported by progressive cerebellar dysfunction, autonomic failure, and characteristic MRI changes — “The progressive cerebellar disorder associated with autonomic dysfunction and typical neuroimaging features of MSA-C lead to a probable diagnosis of MSA-C.”  
2. Alcohol or phenytoin toxicity excluded by the presence of a cruciform pontine sign rather than simple cerebellar flattening — “persistent alcohol consumption and chronic toxicity of Dilantin, which cause cerebellar flattering with no cruciform sign or pontine atrophy.”  
3. Spinocerebellar ataxia subtypes (2, 3, 6) considered but ruled out in the absence of genetic confirmation — “subtypes 2, 3, and 6 of spinocerebellar ataxia may be radiologically comparable to MSA-C, but genetic testing could distinguish the two entities.”  
4. Vasculitis less likely given lack of vessel wall irregularities or focal ischemic zones — “vasculitis usually manifests as irregular vessel walls with zones of ischemia.”  
5. Variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease unlikely due to absence of a pulvinar sign — “variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease presents with a typical pulvinar sign.”
